FAQ
Chainlink ETF flows — common questions
Where does Chainlink ETF flow data come from?
Which Chainlink ETFs are tracked?
How far back does the Chainlink ETF flow history go?

Chainlink ETF flows show how much money moves into and out of U.S. spot Chainlink exchange-traded funds each trading day. No market-data aggregator publishes this series, so the numbers on this page are computed from the issuers' own disclosures.

Inside the Chainlink ETF market

2 U.S. spot Chainlink ETFs trade today: Grayscale GLNK (0.35%, NYSE, listed December 2025); Bitwise CLNK (0.34%, NYSE, listed January 2026). Because fees and launch dates differ, so does each fund's share of the flow — the per-fund table above shows which issuer is actually taking in the money on any given day.

Chainlink is the largest of the newer altcoin ETF markets by assets, and the split between the two funds is lopsided: the Grayscale product, which converted from an existing private trust and therefore started with assets already in it, holds most of the money, while the Bitwise fund has been taking the larger share of new creations since it listed.

A creation means an authorised participant delivered cash or LINK and received new fund shares: money entering the fund. A redemption is the reverse. Summed over time, these creations and redemptions are the cumulative net flow — the clearest available measure of how much regulated capital sits behind Chainlink.

What drives Chainlink ETF inflows and outflows
LINK price momentum: flows into small crypto ETFs are strongly trend-following, and creations cluster after multi-day rallies.
Fee competition: with sponsor fees on these products ranging from zero to 2.50%, assets migrate toward the cheaper wrapper once several funds list on the same asset.
Advisor platform access: a fund only starts collecting steady flow once wirehouses and RIA custodians clear it, which usually happens months after listing.
Basis and arbitrage: authorised participants create shares when the fund trades at a premium to NAV and redeem at a discount, so flow often follows the premium.
Seed and conversion events: the first creation of a fund can dwarf months of ordinary flow, which is why a single day can move the cumulative line more than a quarter of trading.
How to read the data on this page

The daily chart shows net flow in millions of dollars: green is a creation day, red a redemption day, and a flat line means no baskets changed hands. Weekends and U.S. market holidays are absent because ETFs do not create or redeem then.

The cumulative chart adds those days up from the first day of trading, so it answers a different question: not "what happened today" but "how much money has this asset attracted in total". The fund table underneath breaks the same numbers down by issuer, with assets under management and the sponsor fee each fund charges.

Flows are computed daily from primary sources, not copied from another tracker. For each fund we read shares outstanding and net asset value per share straight from the issuer and compute the flow as the change in share count multiplied by that day's NAV, shifted one business day — a creation settles into the share count the following day. Grayscale publishes a daily performance file going back to the birth of the trust, so its entire history is reconstructed from primary data; the Bitwise series is derived from the asset total less the Grayscale fund.
